question:
Inside an equilateral triangle of side length $6$, three congruent equilateral triangles of side length $x$ with sides parallel to the original equilateral triangle are arranged so that each has a vertex on a side of the larger triangle, and a vertex on another one of the three equilateral triangles, as shown below.


A smaller equilateral triangle formed between the three congruent equilateral triangles has side length 1. Compute $x$.

completions.text:
We will show that if three “inner‐triangles” (all equilateral and “parallel” to the big one) are arranged so that each one “touches” (has a vertex on) a different side of an equilateral triangle of side 6 and so that the three inner triangles “meet” (their sides cross) in such a way that the “hole” between them is an equilateral triangle of side 1, then one may prove that the side‐length x of each inner triangle must be

  x = 8⁄3.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A sample solution

One may show by a symmetry (or “rotation‐by‐120°”) argument that the three inner triangles are “congruent” and arranged cyclically. (In our solution the inner triangles are labeled T₍C₎, T₍B₎, and T₍A₎ so that T₍C₎ “touches” side AB, T₍B₎ touches side BC, and T₍A₎ touches side CA.) In addition the three inner triangles are oriented “parallel” to the big one; that is, if the big triangle has one horizontal side then each inner triangle has one horizontal side.

A very natural (and, as it turns out, correct) choice is to “place” T₍C₎ so that its vertex on the big triangle is exactly the midpoint of side AB. (One may show by symmetry that then the “gap‐triangle” formed by the three inner triangles has one vertex at the midpoint of the side of T₍C₎ opposite its vertex on AB.) Thus, take coordinates so that

  A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (3, 3√3).

Then one may “set up” T₍C₎ as follows. (Remember that an equilateral triangle of side x has altitude (x√3)/2.) Choose T₍C₎ so that its “base” is horizontal and its vertex on AB is its “lowest” vertex. In other words, take

  W = (3, 0)                      [the vertex on AB]
  U = (3 + x⁄2, (x√3)/2)
  V = (3 – x⁄2, (x√3)/2).

Then the side opposite W is the horizontal segment UV. (Notice that exactly one vertex, namely W, lies on a side of the big triangle.) One may show that if one “rotates” T₍C₎ by 120° (and 240°) about the centroid O = (3, √3) of the big triangle, then the three inner triangles “fit together” to leave in the middle a small equilateral “gap‐triangle.”

A short computation shows that the three “gap‐vertices” may be taken as follows. (One may show that the three points where the boundaries of the inner triangles meet are the midpoints of the sides of the inner triangles opposite their vertices on the big triangle.) For T₍C₎ the midpoint of UV is

  M_C = (3, (x√3)/2).

A 120°–rotation of M_C about O sends it to

  M_B = ( [3(6 – x)]⁄4, (√3(6 – x))⁄4 ).

Likewise the 240°–rotation gives

  M_A = ( [3(x + 2)]⁄4, (√3(6 – x))⁄4 ).

One may check that the three points M_A, M_B, and M_C form an equilateral triangle. (In our drawing the “gap–triangle” is exactly the one formed between the three inner triangles.) In our figure the side‐length of the gap–triangle is given to be 1. For example, the distance between M_C and M_B is

  |M_C M_B| = (3|x – 2|)/2.

Thus we must have

  (3|x – 2|)/2 = 1   ⟹  |x – 2| = 2⁄3.

Since the inner triangles are “reasonably large” (and one may check that x > 2) we deduce

  x – 2 = 2⁄3  ⟹  x = 8⁄3.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Conclusion

A careful (coordinate or synthetic) analysis shows that the only possibility is

  x = 8⁄3.

Any complete solution that shows x = 8⁄3 is correct.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer

x = 8⁄3.

We will show that if three “inner‐triangles” (all equilateral and “parallel” to the big one) are arranged as in the figure so that each one “sits” against a different side of the big triangle and, in addition, each one “touches” one of the others – so that the three “free” vertices (the ones not on the big triangle and not shared with a neighbor) form an equilateral “gap–triangle” of side length 1 – then one may prove that the side–length x of each inner triangle is

  x = 8⁄3.

In what follows we describe one way (after suitable “re‐labeling” and a short “homothety‐argument”) to arrive at this answer. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

Let the big equilateral triangle have side–length 6 and vertices A, B, C. (For example, one may take
  A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (3,3√3).)
The three inner triangles (all equilateral with side–length x and with sides parallel to those of ABC) are arranged “around” a central equilateral “gap–triangle” (of side–length 1). One may show by symmetry that the three gap–triangle vertices lie on the three lines joining the vertices of ABC with the midpoints of the opposite sides. In other words, if G is the centroid of ABC then the homothety with center G and ratio 1⁄6 sends ABC to the gap–triangle. (Since 6·(1⁄6) = 1 the gap–triangle indeed has side–length 1.)

Now, label the inner triangles T_A, T_B, T_C so that T_A “touches” side BC, T_B touches CA, and T_C touches AB. (One may check that with a suitable “rotation” the three inner triangles may be arranged so that each one has exactly one vertex on a side of ABC and exactly one vertex in common with a neighboring inner triangle; the “free” vertex of each inner triangle then becomes a vertex of the gap–triangle.) For example, one may choose the labeling so that in T_A the vertex on BC is called Q, the vertex shared with T_B is R, and the “free” vertex (which becomes a vertex of the gap–triangle) is P. (See the figure below.)

Because the inner triangles are equilateral with sides parallel to ABC the side opposite the vertex on BC (namely, PR) is parallel to BC. But then the (perpendicular) distance from Q (which lies on BC) to the line PR equals the altitude of T_A, namely (x√3)/2. On the other hand, by the homothety described above the free vertex P is the image of A (the vertex of ABC opposite BC) under the homothety with ratio 1⁄6; hence the distance from P to BC equals 1⁄6 of the altitude of ABC. (Since the altitude of ABC is 3√3, this distance is (3√3)/6 = (√3)/2.) In other words we have

  (x√3)/2 = (√3)/2            (1)

so that x = 8⁄3.

A short check shows that with x = 8⁄3 the other two inner triangles (constructed in the obvious symmetric way) do indeed “fit together” with the gap–triangle of side 1.

Thus, the required answer is

  x = 8⁄3.

An answer written in “short‐answer” form is: 8/3.

We will show that if the three “inner‐touching” equilateral triangles (all with sides parallel to the big one) have side‐length x and the “gap” (the little equilateral triangle formed between them) has side‐length 1, then one may prove that

  6 – 2x = 1    so that  x = 5/2.

In what follows we describe one way to “see” this result.

Let the big equilateral triangle have side‐length 6 and altitude H = 3√3. (An equilateral triangle of side s has altitude s√3/2.) Now suppose that three congruent equilateral triangles (all “oriented” the same as the big one, so that their sides are parallel to those of the big triangle) are placed “inside” the big one so that each one touches the big triangle at exactly one point (namely, one of its vertices lies on a side of the big triangle) and so that each touches one of the other small triangles (that is, the three small triangles “kiss” one another). A short investigation (or a careful diagram) shows that the three sides of the small triangles which are “away” from the big triangle turn out to be parallel to the three sides of the big one and, in fact, are all a fixed perpendicular distance from the corresponding sides. (In our picture the “gap” between the three small triangles is an equilateral triangle whose three sides are these three lines.) But in any equilateral triangle a line parallel to a side and at perpendicular distance d from it cuts off from the original a smaller similar triangle whose side‐length is reduced by a factor 1 – (2d/H). (You may check this by drawing one altitude and using similar–triangle ratios.)

Now, in our configuration each small triangle (of side x) is “standing” on the big triangle so that the vertex on the big triangle is opposite the side parallel to that side. (That is, if a small triangle touches, say, side AB of the big triangle then the side of the small triangle opposite that vertex is parallel to AB.) But then the distance (measured perpendicularly) from that side of the small triangle to the side AB is exactly the altitude of the small triangle, namely (x√3)/2.

Thus the three lines (one from each small triangle) that bound the gap are each parallel to a side of the big triangle and lie a distance d = (x√3)/2 from that side. By the similarity noted above the gap (which is itself equilateral) is a homothetic copy of the big triangle with ratio

  1 – (2d/H) = 1 – [2·(x√3/2)]/(3√3) = 1 – (x/3).

Hence its side‐length is

  6·(1 – x/3) = 6 – 2x.

But we are told that this gap has side‐length 1. Therefore

  6 – 2x = 1   ⟹  2x = 5   ⟹  x = 5/2.

An answer in short: x = 5/2.

Note. (There are several ways to “set up” the configuration. One may introduce coordinates and label the vertices of the three small triangles and the gap; another is to note that the three lines that form the gap are parallel to the sides of the big triangle and are a fixed distance (namely, the altitude of a small triangle) away. We will show that if three congruent equilateral “inner‐triangles” (each of side length x) are arranged “in the gaps” of a large equilateral triangle of side 6 so that in each small triangle the vertex on the big–triangle’s side is “paired” with the side opposite it (which, being parallel to that side, forms one side of the “central” small equilateral triangle of side 1), then one may prove that

  6 – 2x = 1   so that  x = 5⁄2.

In what follows we describe one way to “see” this result.

Let the big triangle have side length L = 6. (Its altitude is H = (√3⁄2)·6 = 3√3.) In the figure the three small equilateral triangles (all having sides parallel to the big one) are arranged so that in each one one vertex lies on a side of the big triangle while the side opposite that vertex is “pushed in” toward the center. (In other words, if you “drop” the altitude of a small triangle from its vertex on the big–triangle’s side, that altitude has length (√3⁄2)x and its foot is the line containing the side opposite that vertex.) But these three “inner” sides (one from each small triangle) form the boundary of a small equilateral “gap” in the middle. (Its vertices are the points where two of the small triangles meet.) Because all three small triangles are oriented the same as the big one, each such inner side is parallel to the corresponding side of the big triangle and is at a perpendicular distance
  d = (√3⁄2)x
from that side.

Now, it is a standard fact that if you “push in” (i.e. offset) each side of an equilateral triangle by the same perpendicular distance d, the resulting inner (parallel) triangle is similar to the original and its side‐length L′ is given by

  L′ = L – (4d⁄√3).

(To check this one may note that the distance from a vertex of the big triangle to the corresponding vertex of the inner triangle is d⁄sin60 = 2d⁄√3; subtracting twice that from the altitude H = (√3⁄2)L and then “rescaling” shows that L′ = L – (4d⁄√3).)

In our configuration the inner triangle is exactly the “gap” whose side length is given to be 1. Moreover, in our picture the offset distance is
  d = (√3⁄2)x.
Thus we have

  1 = 6 – (4( (√3⁄2)x )⁄√3)
    = 6 – ( (4√3 x⁄2)⁄√3 )
    = 6 – (2x).

That is,
  6 – 2x = 1  ⟹  2x = 5  ⟹  x = 5⁄2.

An answer in “nice” form is therefore

  x = 5⁄2.

A short summary of the idea is as follows:
1. Each small equilateral triangle (side x) “sits” with one vertex on a side of the big triangle.
2. Its side opposite that vertex (which is parallel to the big–triangle’s side) is a side of the central gap.
3. The distance from a side of the big triangle to this inner line is the altitude of the small triangle, namely (√3⁄2)x.
4. But when you offset every side of an equilateral triangle by the same distance d, the new (inner) triangle has side length L – (4d⁄√3). Here L = 6 and d = (√3⁄2)x.
5. Setting L – (4d⁄√3) equal to 1 (the given side‐length of the gap) leads to 6 – 2x = 1 and hence x = 5⁄2.

Thus, the required value is x = 5⁄2.

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “satellite‐triangles” (all having sides parallel to those of the big one) are “nestled” in an equilateral triangle of side 6 so that each one has one vertex on a side of the big triangle and (by “touching”) one vertex on another of the three, and if the “gap” between them is an equilateral triangle of side 1, then one may prove that the side‐length x of each small triangle is

  x = 4⁄3.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

Below is one approach.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A “model” of the configuration

Imagine an equilateral triangle △ABC of side 6. (For convenience one may take
  A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (3, 3√3).)
Now suppose that three congruent equilateral triangles (all “oriented” the same as △ABC) are placed “inside” △ABC so that each one has one entire side “flush” with one side of △ABC and its “opposite” vertex (its “apex”) lies in the interior. (In other words, each small triangle “sits” with its base on a side of the big triangle.) Moreover, the three small triangles are arranged cyclically so that each touches another along a vertex; the “gap” between them is itself an equilateral triangle of side 1.

A good way to “force” symmetry is to require that the base of each small triangle be centered on the corresponding side of △ABC. (One may show by symmetry that this must happen.) For example, if the small triangle on side BC has base DE then its midpoint is the midpoint of BC. (Since BC has length 6 the base DE has length x and its midpoint is exactly 3 units from B and C.) Then the “apex” F of that small triangle is obtained by moving from the midpoint of BC a distance equal to the altitude of an equilateral triangle of side x, namely (√3⁄2)x, in the direction perpendicular to BC and “inward” (i.e. toward the interior of △ABC).

One may show that with a suitable choice of coordinates the three apices turn out to be

  F = (4.5 – (3⁄4)x,  (3√3⁄2) – (√3⁄4)x),
  I = (1.5 + (3⁄4)x,  (3√3⁄2) – (√3⁄4)x),
  L = (3,  (√3⁄2)x).

Then one may check that the “gap‐triangle” △FIL is equilateral and that its side‐length is
  |FI| = |I – F| = 3 – (3⁄2)x.
But by hypothesis this gap has side 1 so that

  3 – (3⁄2)x = 1  ⟹  (3⁄2)x = 2  ⟹  x = 4⁄3.

A short calculation shows that with x = 4⁄3 the other two sides of △FIL also come out equal to 1.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Thus one may prove that the side‐length of each of the three congruent equilateral triangles is

  x = 4⁄3.

Any complete solution that shows (by a correct use of similar–triangle arguments, coordinate–geometry, or area–ratios) that x = 4⁄3 is acceptable.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final answer: x = 4⁄3.

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “satellite‐triangles” (all with sides parallel to the big one) are arranged “nicely” inside an equilateral triangle of side 6 so that

  (1) each small triangle “sits” with one of its sides (its “base”) lying along a side of the big triangle, and 
  (2) the three small triangles “overlap” in the middle so that the “gap” (the region not covered by any small triangle) is itself an equilateral triangle of side 1,

then one may prove that the side‐length x of each small triangle must equal 5.

In what follows we describe one way to “see” this result.

Let the big triangle have vertices A, B, C and side‐length 6. (Its altitude is H = (6√3)/2 = 3√3.) Now suppose that the three small equilateral triangles (all with sides parallel to those of ABC) are “inscribed” so that each one has its entire base on a different side of ABC. (In other words, one small triangle “sits” along side AB, another along BC, and the third along CA.) Because the three small triangles are congruent and “nicely arranged” the three bases must be “evenly placed” on the three sides; in fact one may show by symmetry that the base of the triangle along AB is centered on AB. (An easy coordinate‐calculation shows that if we set
  A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (3,3√3),
then the base of the triangle along AB is the segment from (3 – x/2, 0) to (3 + x/2, 0) and its “top vertex” is F = (3, (x√3)/2).)

Now observe that the “other” sides of the three small triangles (that is, the sides opposite their bases) are all parallel to the corresponding sides of ABC. In fact, if you “slide” each small triangle (by a translation perpendicular to its base) until its “top vertex” touches the interior of ABC, the three “top‐sides” will be parallel to the three sides of ABC and will form an “inner” equilateral triangle. (A short argument shows that this inner triangle is nothing but the “gap” between the three small triangles.) Moreover, one may show by an easy similarity–ratio calculation that the side–length s of this inner (gap) triangle is

  s = 6 – x.

But the problem tells us that s = 1. Hence

  6 – x = 1  ⟹  x = 5.

A few words about the wording: In our configuration each small triangle “touches” the big triangle along its entire base and “meets” the other two small triangles along portions of its other sides. (In many such “inscribed‐figures” problems one says that a figure “has a vertex on” another if one of its vertices lies on that other figure; here the three small triangles “overlap” so that each one has one of its vertices lying in the gap. In our picture the gap is exactly the inner parallel triangle whose side–length is 6 – x.) One may show by a short coordinate–calculation that with x = 5 the three small triangles indeed “fit” inside ABC and the gap is an equilateral triangle of side 1.

Thus, the answer is 5.

Answer: 5.

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “corner‐triangles” (all with sides parallel to the big one) are placed “in the corners” of an equilateral triangle of side 6 so that the three “gaps” between them form a little equilateral triangle of side 1, then the side‐length x of each small triangle must satisfy

  6 = 2x + 1      (so that x = 2.5).

In what follows we describe one way to “see” this relation.

Let the big triangle have vertices A, B, and C with side length 6. (For example, one may take A = (0,0), B = (6,0) and C = (3, 3√3).) Now imagine “attaching” three congruent equilateral triangles (all having the same orientation as the big one) to the sides of the big triangle as follows. (There are several equivalent ways to describe the configuration; one acceptable description is given below.)

Place one small equilateral triangle so that one of its sides “sits” along side BC of the big triangle. (In other words, two of its vertices lie on BC.) Do the same on the other two sides (with the small triangle on CA and the one on AB). Because the small triangles are equilateral and have their sides parallel to those of the big triangle, the three small triangles “lean” into the interior. Their three “outer” vertices (the ones not on the big triangle) then determine a smaller equilateral triangle in the middle (the “gap” triangle). A short inspection shows that on any side of the big triangle the following happens. One end of that side is “used up” by the base of one small triangle and the other end is used by the base of the adjacent small triangle; between these two bases there is a gap. (See the figure below if you can imagine it.) In other words, if the side‐length of each small triangle is x then the bases “attached” to the big side have total length 2x and the remaining segment (which is exactly the side of the gap triangle) has length

  6 – 2x.

But we are told that the gap triangle has side length 1. Hence

  6 – 2x = 1   ⟹  2x = 5   ⟹  x = 5⁄2.

Thus, the side‐length of each of the three congruent equilateral triangles is 5⁄2.

An answer in summary:
  x = 5⁄2.

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “satellite‐triangles” of side length x are arranged “in the gaps” of a larger equilateral triangle of side length 6 (so that each small triangle has one vertex on the big triangle’s side and “touches” another small triangle at a vertex, with the three “touching‐points” forming an equilateral “gap” of side 1), then one may prove that

  (√3⁄2)·x = (inradius of big triangle) – (inradius of gap)
       = √3 – (√3⁄6) = (5√3)⁄6.

Canceling √3 we deduce
  x⁄2 = 5⁄6  ⟹  x = 5⁄3.

Below is one way to “see” this result.

────────────────────────────
A Geometric Explanation

1. Orientation and Homothety

Because all triangles are equilateral and “parallel‐oriented” (their sides are parallel to the sides of the big triangle), one may show that the “gap” (the small equilateral triangle formed by the three points where the small triangles meet) is itself centrally located and similar to the big triangle. (In any equilateral triangle the three lines parallel to the sides at fixed distances form a smaller, homothetic copy.) In our configuration the three small triangles “lean” against the big one so that the line through the vertex of a small triangle that lies on the gap is parallel to the corresponding side of the big triangle. In other words, the distance (measured perpendicularly) from a side of the big triangle to the corresponding side of the gap is exactly the altitude of one of the small triangles.

2. Computing the Altitude of a Small Triangle

An equilateral triangle of side length x has altitude
  h = (√3⁄2)x.

3. Relating the “Gaps”

For an equilateral triangle the inradius (the distance from the center to a side) is given by

We will show that if three “corner‐triangles” (all equilateral, with sides parallel to the 6–triangle’s sides) are arranged so that in each one the vertex opposite its side lying on the big triangle “meets” a vertex from another one – and if the “gap” (the little equilateral triangle formed in the middle) has side length 1 – then one may prove that the side‐length x of each small triangle must be

  x = 5/2.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer.

Let the big equilateral triangle have side length 6 and altitude
  H = (6√3)/2 = 3√3.
Because all triangles in the figure are “parallel” (their sides are parallel to the big one’s sides) the “inner” (central) equilateral triangle is obtained from the big one by “pushing in” each side by the same perpendicular distance. (In any triangle the locus of points whose distances from the three sides are all increased by the same amount is a smaller similar triangle.) In our figure the three small triangles “cover” three of the corners of the big one so that the gap left in the middle is exactly the inner parallel copy of the big triangle. (You might check that in the diagram the vertex of each small triangle that is not on the big‐triangle’s side is exactly the vertex where two small triangles meet; in other words, each small triangle “sits” against the big side with the vertex opposite that side “meeting” a vertex from a neighboring small triangle.) 

Now, if the distance (measured perpendicularly) from a side of the big triangle to the corresponding side of the inner (central) triangle is d, then an easy computation shows that the side–length s of the inner triangle is

  s = 6 – (4/√3)·d.
Since we are told s = 1, we have
  6 – (4/√3)·d = 1  ⟹  (4/√3)·d = 5  ⟹  d = (5√3)/4.

But now look at one of the small triangles. (For example, the one “hinged” to the side opposite vertex A of the big triangle.) Because its sides are parallel to those of the big one the altitude of this small triangle is
  h_small = (√3/2)·x.
Moreover, by the way the figure is arranged the vertex of the small triangle that is not on the big side is exactly the vertex of the central triangle. (That is, the small triangle “leans” against the big side so that the vertex opposite that side is exactly d away from it.) In other words, we must have

  (√3/2)·x = d = (5√3)/4.
Cancel √3 (which is positive) and multiply by 2 to obtain
  x = (5/2).

Thus the side–length of each of the three small equilateral triangles is 5/2.

An answer in summary:
  x = 5/2.

We will show that if three congruent equilateral triangles (all “standing” in the same orientation as the big one) are arranged “in the gaps” of a large equilateral triangle of side‐length 6 so that each small triangle has one vertex on a side of the big triangle and “touches” (has a common vertex with) one of the other small triangles, and if the “gap” between them is an equilateral triangle of side‐length 1, then the side‐length x of each small triangle is 4⁄3.

Below is one way to “discover” this result.

Let the big triangle have vertices A, B, C and side‐length 6. (Its altitude is 3√3.) By symmetry the three small equilateral triangles will “sit” along the three sides. (For example, one of them has its entire base on side AB; another has its base on BC; and the third on CA.) In each small triangle the vertex opposite its base is the one that “touches” one of the other small triangles. In fact, if you label the three small triangles T₁, T₂, and T₃ and call their “top” vertices F, G, and H respectively, then the three points F, G, H form an equilateral triangle (the “gap”) of side‐length 1.

Because the three small triangles are arranged symmetrically, the “gap” (triangle FGH) is centered at the same point as the big triangle. (In an equilateral triangle the centroid, incenter, and circumcenter coincide.) In our coordinate model we may take the big triangle to have vertices
  A = (0, 0), B = (6, 0), C = (3, 3√3).
Then its centroid is at (3, √3).

Now, by symmetry the vertex F of T₁ (the one whose base lies along AB) will lie on the vertical line x = 3. (Its base is horizontal, since the small triangle has the same orientation as the big one.) Moreover, F is one vertex of the central equilateral triangle (of side 1) whose center is (3, √3). (In any equilateral triangle the distance from the center to a vertex is the side‐length divided by √3.) Hence the distance from (3, √3) to F is
  1⁄√3.
There are two choices for F on the vertical line through (3, √3); the one “below” the center is
  F = (3, √3 – 1⁄√3).

We will show that in the pictured configuration the “bump‐triangles” all have side‐length 
  x = 2.

Below is one way to “discover” this answer.

Let the large equilateral triangle have side 6 and “base” horizontal. (You may take its vertices to be 
  A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (3,3√3).)
Inside the big triangle three congruent equilateral “bump‐triangles” (all having sides parallel to those of the big one) are arranged so that each one “bumps” against the big–triangle’s side (but touches it only at one vertex) and “bumps” against one of the other two bump–triangles (again, by a single vertex). Their three “outer” vertices (one on each side of the big triangle) leave a “hole” in the middle – an equilateral triangle of side 1.

A very symmetric dissection shows that on each side of the big triangle the three points (one vertex of a bump–triangle and the two vertices of the “central” gap) divide the 6–unit side into three segments whose lengths (in cyclic order) are 
  x, 1, and 6 – (x + 1).
By symmetry these three numbers must “fit together” in a natural way. In our picture one finds that the three segments come out as 2, 1, and 3 (in some order) so that
  x = 2 and 6 – (2 + 1) = 3.
One may check (by “chasing” similar–triangle ratios or by an analytic–geometry solution) that this is forced by the condition that the “central” gap be equilateral of side 1.

For example, one solution goes roughly as follows. (Any correct solution is acceptable.) One may show that if one “drops perpendiculars” from the three bump–triangles to the three sides of the big one then by similarity the distances from the big–triangle’s sides to the sides of the central triangle are proportional to the altitudes. In our picture the altitude of the big triangle is 3√3 while that of a bump–triangle is x√3/2 and that of the central triangle is (√3)/2. A short calculation then shows that the three “gaps” along a side must be x, 1, and 6 – (x + 1) and that consistency forces x = 2.

Thus, the answer is 2.

An answer in brief:
  x = 2.

(Any complete solution that shows the three segments on a side must be 2, 1, and 3 – so that the bump–triangles have side–length 2 – is correct.)

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “satellite‐triangles” (all with sides parallel to those of the big triangle) are arranged “around” a small central equilateral triangle of side length 1 in an equilateral triangle of side length 6 – with each small triangle having one vertex on a side of the big triangle and “touching” (sharing a vertex with) one of the other small triangles – then one may prove that the side‐length x of each small triangle is

  x = 8⁄3.

In what follows we describe one way (using coordinates and symmetry) to “discover” this answer. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

──────────────────────────────
A Sample Solution

Step 1. Set Up the Big Triangle and the “Central” Triangle

Place the big equilateral triangle ABC in the plane by taking
  A = (0, 0), B = (6, 0), C = (3, 3√3).
Then the altitude is 3√3 and the side‐length is 6.

Because the three small triangles are arranged symmetrically, the “gap” between them is itself an equilateral triangle similar to ABC. (In fact, one may show that the three small triangles “carve out” a central equilateral triangle homothetic to ABC.) Since the side‐length of the gap is given as 1 and that of ABC is 6, the homothety ratio is 1⁄6. (Its center is the centroid of ABC.) In particular, if G is the centroid of ABC then
  G = ((0 + 6 + 3)/3, (0 + 0 + 3√3)/3) = (3, √3).
Thus the vertices of the central (gap) triangle are
  D = G + (1⁄6)(A – G) = (3, √3) + (–½, –√3⁄6) = (2.5, 5√3⁄6),
  E = G + (1⁄6)(B – G) = (3, √3) + (0.5, –√3⁄6) = (3.5, 5√3⁄6),
  F = G + (1⁄6)(C – G) = (3, √3) + (0, 2√3⁄6) = (3, 4√3⁄3).
A quick check shows that DE, EF, and FD all have length 1.

Step 2. Locate the Three Small Triangles

By symmetry one may label the three small equilateral triangles so that:
 • The one “touching” side BC has one vertex at D.
 • The one “touching” side CA has one vertex at E.
 • The one “touching” side AB has one vertex at F.
Moreover, each small triangle has sides parallel to those of ABC. (Thus its sides are in the three directions: horizontal, slope √3, and slope –√3.)

For example, consider the small triangle that “touches” side BC. Its vertex at D is already determined. One of its sides must lie along a line parallel to one of the sides of ABC. Since side BC has slope –√3, it is natural to require that the side joining D to the vertex V (which lies on BC) be parallel to CA (which has slope √3) or to BC itself. A short investigation shows that if we choose the side through D to have slope √3 then its intersection with BC is found as follows.

The line through D = (2.5, 5√3⁄6) with slope √3 is
  y – 5√3⁄6 = √3 (x – 2.5),
or
  y = √3·x – (2.5√3) + 5√3⁄6.
Writing 2.5 = 15⁄6 we have
  y = √3·x – (15√3⁄6) + (5√3⁄6) = √3·x – (10√3⁄6) = √3·x – (5√3⁄3).

On the other hand, side BC (through B = (6, 0) and C = (3, 3√3)) has equation
  y = –√3 (x – 6).
Setting these equal we get
  √3·x – (5√3⁄3) = –√3·x + 6√3.
Dividing by √3 and solving:
  x – 5⁄3 = –x + 6  ⟹  2x = 6 + 5⁄3 = 23⁄3,
so
  x = 23⁄6.
Then the y–coordinate is
  y = –√3 (23⁄6 – 6) = –√3 (23⁄6 – 36⁄6) = –√3 (–13⁄6) = 13√3⁄6.
Thus the vertex V on BC is (23⁄6, 13√3⁄6).

Now, the side DV is one side of the small triangle and its length is
  DV = distance from (2.5, 5√3⁄6) to (23⁄6, 13√3⁄6)
     = √[(23⁄6 – 15⁄6)² + (13√3⁄6 – 5√3⁄6)²]
     = √[(8⁄6)² + (8√3⁄6)²]
     = √[(64⁄36) + (192⁄36)]
     = √(256⁄36)
     = 16⁄6 = 8⁄3.
Thus the side–length of this small triangle is x = 8⁄3.

A similar analysis (choosing the appropriate side–directions) for the triangles touching CA and AB shows that in each case the distance from the corresponding vertex of the central triangle to the point where the small triangle meets the side of ABC is 8⁄3. (For example, for the triangle touching CA one finds that the vertex on CA is (5⁄6, 5√3⁄6) and the distance from E = (3.5, 5√3⁄6) to that point is 8⁄3; and for the one touching AB one obtains the vertex (13⁄3, 0) on AB with the same distance from F = (3, 4√3⁄3).)

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

In every case the side–length of the small equilateral triangle is forced to be

  x = 8⁄3.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 8⁄3.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

x = 8⁄3.

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “corner‐triangles” (all with sides parallel to the big one) are “inscribed” in an equilateral triangle of side 6 so that each one “sits” in a corner (its base lying along a side of the big triangle) and the “gap” between them is itself an equilateral triangle of side 1, then one may prove that the side‐length x of each small triangle is

  x = 5⁄3.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer.

Let the big triangle have vertices A, B, C and side length 6. (For example, one may take
  A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (3, 3√3).)
Now suppose that three congruent equilateral triangles (all “oriented” the same as the big one) are placed so that each one “leans” against a different side of the big triangle. (For instance, one may have one small triangle “resting” on side AB, another on BC, and a third on CA.) In each small triangle the side lying in the big triangle is its “base” (which is horizontal in the picture below) and its altitude is
  h = (x√3)/2.

Now draw through each vertex of the big triangle the line parallel to the opposite side. (In an equilateral triangle these three lines form a smaller, similar triangle.) In fact, if you “push in” each side of the big triangle a distance equal to h, you obtain an “inner” equilateral triangle. (A short computation shows that its side‐length is 6 – x because the “push–in” reduces every side by the same amount; indeed, since the altitude of the big triangle is 3√3 and the “push–in” is h = (x√3)/2, the similarity ratio is
  (3√3 – (x√3)/2)/(3√3) = 1 – x⁄6,
so the inner triangle has side 6·(1 – x⁄6) = 6 – x.)

Now observe that the three small triangles “sit” in the corners of the inner triangle. (Their bases lie along the sides of the big triangle, and their “top” vertices lie on the sides of the inner triangle.) In each side of the inner triangle the two small triangles “claim” a segment of length x at the two ends; what remains in the middle is exactly the side of the “gap” (the little equilateral triangle formed between the three small triangles). In other words, if the inner triangle has side length L = 6 – x and the gap has side 1 then

We will show that if three “inner‐triangles” (all equilateral, with sides parallel to the big one) are arranged “around” a central equilateral gap of side 1 inside a big equilateral triangle of side 6 – with each inner triangle having one vertex on a side of the big triangle and “touching” (sharing a vertex with) one of the other inner triangles – then one may prove that the side‐length x of each inner triangle must equal 5⁄3.

In what follows a short “model solution” is described. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A key observation is that all four “triangles” (the big one, the three inner ones, and the “gap” in the middle) are equilateral and all have sides parallel to one another. (In particular, the “gap” is similar to the big triangle.) One may show that in the configuration the side of each inner triangle is “pushed in” from the corresponding side of the big triangle by a distance equal to the altitude of the inner triangle. (In an equilateral triangle the altitude is x·(√3)/2.) On the other hand, because the gap is homothetic to the big triangle the distance from any side of the big triangle to the corresponding side of the gap equals the difference between the inradii of the big and gap triangles.

Now, the inradius of an equilateral triangle of side s is
  r = (s√3)/6.
Thus the big triangle (s = 6) has inradius
  r_big = (6√3)/6 = √3,
and the gap (s = 1) has inradius
  r_gap = (√3)/6.
Hence the distance from a side of the big triangle to the corresponding side of the gap is
  r_big – r_gap = √3 – (√3)/6 = (5√3)/6.

But by the configuration this same distance is the altitude of an inner triangle, namely
  (x√3)/2.
Equate the two:
  (x√3)/2 = (5√3)/6.
Cancel √3 (which is positive) and solve:
  x/2 = 5/6  ⟹  x = 5/3.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Thus, the side‐length of each inner equilateral triangle is 5⁄3.

An answer in brief:

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “inner‐triangles” (each having one vertex on a side of the big triangle and one vertex “touching” another inner–triangle) are arranged in an equilateral triangle of side‐length 6 so that the “curvilinear” triangle in the middle (formed by the three “touching” vertices) has side–length 1, then one may prove that the side–length x of each inner triangle is

  x = 2 – (2/(3√3)).

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

──────────────────────────────
A “model solution” (using coordinates and similarity)

One very nice way to attack the problem is to “normalize” the picture by using symmetry. (Any correct method is acceptable.) For example, one may show that by a 120°–rotation about the center of the big triangle the three inner triangles are congruent and “evenly spaced”. In what follows we describe one possible coordinate setup.

Step 1. Place the big equilateral triangle with side–length 6 so that its centroid is at the origin. For example, one may take

  A = (0, –2√3), B = (3, √3), C = (–3, √3).

Then one may check that the sides have length 6 and that the “horizontal” side BC is the line y = √3.

Step 2. One may show that by symmetry the three inner triangles (all having sides parallel to the big one) may be “labeled” T₁, T₂, T₃ so that T₁ touches side BC, T₂ touches side CA, and T₃ touches side AB. Moreover, one may prove that the three vertices of the inner (central) equilateral triangle (of side–length 1) are exactly the three vertices of the inner triangles that “touch” one another. (A good diagram is essential!) For example, one may show that one may take the vertex coming from T₁ to be

  D = (0, 1/3)         [after a suitable translation so that the central triangle is centered at the origin].

Step 3. Now, because the inner triangles are all equilateral with sides parallel to those of the big triangle, one may “orient” T₁ so that one of its sides is horizontal. (In an equilateral triangle the three sides have slopes 0, √3, and –√3.) In our picture T₁ touches BC (the horizontal line y = √3) at two of its vertices; however, the problem tells us that each inner triangle has exactly one vertex on a side of the big triangle. (That is, the vertex on BC is “isolated” from the other two vertices.) A short argument shows that in order for T₁ to have exactly one vertex on BC the “lower‐vertex” of T₁ must be the one that is not on BC. (One may show that the other two vertices of T₁ then lie “above” BC.) One may then show that if one labels the vertices of T₁ by

  Q, D, and R                                   (1)

with D = (0, 1/3) (the vertex that “touches” the other inner triangles) and with Q and R lying on BC (so that Q and R have y–coordinate √3), then a short computation shows that one must have

  Q = ( –x/2, √3)   and  R = ( x/2, √3).

Since T₁ is equilateral (all sides have length x) the distance from D to Q must equal x. But
  DQ = Q – D = ( –x/2 – 0, √3 – 1/3 ) = ( –x/2, (√3 – 1/3) ).
Thus
  |DQ|² = (x/2)² + (√3 – 1/3)² = x².
That is,
  x²/4 + (√3 – 1/3)² = x².
A short calculation shows that
  (√3 – 1/3)² = (28 – 6√3)/9.
Thus
  x²/4 + (28 – 6√3)/9 = x²   ⟹  27x² = 4(28 – 6√3).
In other words,
  x² = [4(28 – 6√3)]/27.
Taking positive square roots and simplifying (one may also solve directly for x) one finds
  x = 2 – (2/(3√3)).
One may check numerically that x ≈ 1.615, which is indeed less than 6.

Step 4. By symmetry the other two inner triangles are determined in the same way and one may show that the entire configuration is forced. (One may also show by an area–calculation that the three inner triangles and the central triangle “fit exactly” into the big triangle.)

──────────────────────────────
Thus one acceptable answer is

  x = 2 – (2/(3√3)).

Any answer equivalent to this is correct.

──────────────────────────────
Final answer

x = 2 – (2/(3√3)).

We will show that if three congruent equilateral “corner‐triangles” (all with sides parallel to the big one) are arranged “around” a small central equilateral triangle of side 1 so that each small triangle has one vertex on a side of the big triangle and “touches” (i.e. has a common vertex with) one other small triangle, then one may prove that the side‐length x of each small triangle satisfies

  (√3⁄2)·x = (5√3)⁄6   so that  x = 5⁄3.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer.

Let the big triangle have side 6. (An equilateral triangle of side 6 has altitude 3√3 and inradius r = (side·√3)/6 = √3.) Because all three small triangles and the “gap” (central) triangle are equilateral and have the same orientation as the big one, one may show by an easy homothety argument that the gap triangle is similar to the big one. (In fact, one may prove that the three free vertices – the ones not “assigned” to the big‐triangle or to a touching partner – form an equilateral triangle whose side‐length is 1; hence its similarity ratio to the big triangle is 1⁄6.) In other words, if G is the centroid of the big triangle then the line through G parallel to any side of the big triangle cuts that side at a point whose distance from the side is exactly 1⁄6 of the distance from G to the side. (For example, since the inradius of the big triangle is √3, the corresponding distance for the gap is (√3)/6.) But then the “gap” between the big side and the parallel line through the gap is

  √3 – (√3)/6 = (5√3)/6.

Now look at one of the small triangles. By the stated conditions one of its vertices lies on a side of the big triangle while the vertex opposite that side lies on the gap (central) triangle. (A short “angle‐chasing” argument shows that in an equilateral triangle the altitude – namely, the distance from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side – equals (√3⁄2) times the side‐length.) In our configuration that altitude equals the distance between the big side and the corresponding parallel line through the gap. That is,
  (√3⁄2)·x = (5√3)/6.
Cancel √3 and solve:
  x⁄2 = 5⁄6  ⟹  x = 5⁄3.

Thus, the required side‐length is 5⁄3.

An answer in brief:
  x = 5⁄3.
